Fascial Spaces of the Head & Neck

The fascial layers, the cervical and facial spaces, what each contains and communicates with, and how odontogenic infection spreads.

Lecture 13 · Part 1Fascia of the Head & Neck

Lecturer: Dr Shaoyu Wang, PhD, BVetMed — Senior Lecturer in Anatomy and Physiology. Updated from Dr Yin Shi Chang's 2017 notes.

Fascia: layers of connective tissue that underlie the skin and surround or lie between the muscles, bones, organs, vessels and nerves.

Superficial fasciaDeep fascia
PositionJust deep to and attached to the skin; separates skin from deep structuresCovers the deeper structures of the head and neck
CompositionFat plus irregularly arranged connective tissue, nerves and vesselsDense, inelastic fibrous tissue
BehaviourVaries in thickness in different parts of the bodyForms sheaths around deeper structures

Fascia in the head

  • Superficial fascia encloses the muscles of facial expression and platysma
  • Deep fascia is continuous with the deep cervical fascia and divides into:
DivisionCovers
TemporalThe temporalis muscle and structures superior to the zygomatic arch
Masseteric-parotidThe masseter and structures inferior to the zygomatic arch
PterygoidThe medial surface of the medial pterygoid

Deep cervical fascia

LayerDescription
1. Investing fasciaThe most external layer. Surrounds the neck and continues onto the masseteric-parotid fascia. Splits around 2 salivary glands (submandibular and parotid) and 2 muscles (sternocleidomastoid and trapezius)
2. Carotid sheathA tube of deep cervical fascia lying deep to the investing fascia and SCM
3. Visceral (pretracheal) fasciaDeep and parallel to the carotid sheath, running inferiorly. Surrounds the air and food passageway — trachea, oesophagus and thyroid gland
4. Buccopharyngeal fasciaThe visceral fascia located posterior and lateral to the pharynx, nearer the skull
5. Vertebral (prevertebral) fasciaThe deepest layer. Covers the vertebrae, spinal column and associated muscles
An easy way to hold the five layers: work from the outside in — investing wraps everything, the carotid sheath is a tube within it, visceral fascia hugs the airway and gut tube, buccopharyngeal is that same visceral layer behind the pharynx, and prevertebral is the innermost, against the spine.

Lecture 13 · Part 2Cervical Fascial Spaces

  • Fascial spaces are potential spaces between fascial layers
  • The cervical spaces communicate with each other and with the spaces of the face and jaws
  • They connect the spaces of the face and jaws with those of the thorax
  • This allows odontogenic infection to spread to vital organs — heart, lungs and brain
The three cervical spaces
ParapharyngealRetropharyngealPrevisceral
This is the whole point of the lecture. A space is only "potential" until infection opens it up. Because these spaces are continuous, an untreated dental abscess has an anatomical road from a lower molar to the mediastinum — which is why deep neck infection is treated as an emergency.

Parapharyngeal (lateral pharyngeal) space

Located bilaterally lateral to the pharynx and medial to the medial pterygoid, running parallel to the carotid sheath.

Boundaries

  • Medial: lateral wall of the pharynx
  • Lateral: medial pterygoid and the parotid gland
  • Posterior: carotid sheath / styloid apparatus
  • Superior: base of the skull

Contents

  • Carotid arteries, jugular veins
  • Glossopharyngeal, vagus, hypoglossal and accessory nerves
  • Sympathetic chain
  • Lymph nodes

Communicates with

Submandibular spaceSublingual spaceRetropharyngeal space Thoracic inletCarotid sheathParavertebral muscles

Retropharyngeal space

Located immediately posterior to the pharynx, between the vertebral and visceral fascia.

Boundaries

  • Superior: skull base
  • Anterior: posterior wall of the pharynx
  • Posterior: prevertebral muscles
  • Lateral: carotid sheath

Communicates with

  • Parapharyngeal space
  • Thoracic inlet

Pretracheal (previsceral) space

  • Located between the visceral and investing fasciae, anterior to the trachea
  • Communicates with the parapharyngeal spaces

Lecture 13 · Part 3Spaces of the Face & Jaws

  • They communicate with each other and with the cervical fascial spaces
  • This allows spread of odontogenic infection from a superficial area in the face and jaws to deeper vital structures in the neck, or even the brain
The major spaces
BuccalCanineParotidMasticator SubmentalSubmandibularSublingual

The masticator space is a general term covering the temporal, infratemporal, pterygomandibular and submasseteric spaces.

Buccal space

Formed between the buccinator muscle (buccopharyngeal fascia) and the masseter muscle.

Location

  • Superior: the mandible below, zygomatic arch above
  • Lateral to buccinator
  • Medial and anterior to masseter

Contents

  • Buccal fat pad
  • Parotid duct
  • Facial artery

Communicates with

  • Canine space
  • Pterygomandibular space
  • Submasseteric space
Where a buccal abscess comes from: infection from an upper or lower molar whose root apex lies buccal to the attachment of buccinator drains into this space, producing the classic swollen cheek that does not respect the jaw line.

Canine space

A thin potential space between levator anguli oris and levator labii superioris.

Boundaries

  • Superior: levator labii superioris alaeque nasi, zygomaticus major
  • Anterior: orbicularis oris
  • Posterior: buccinator
  • Floor: the canine fossa

Contents & communications

  • Connective tissue, fat, infra-orbital vessels and nerves
  • Communicates with the buccal space and — critically — the cavernous sinus
The dangerous one. The canine space communicates directly with the cavernous sinus via the ophthalmic veins. An infected upper canine — the tooth with the longest root, whose apex can sit above the origin of levator anguli oris — is the classic source of a canine space infection, and the route to cavernous sinus thrombosis. This is the same "danger triangle" you met in the blood supply and sinus lectures.

Parotid space

Formed inside the investing fascial layer of the deep cervical fascia.

Parotid salivary glandFacial nerve External carotid arteryRetromandibular vein

Lecture 13 · Part 4The Masticator Space

A general term for the entire area of the mandible and the muscles of mastication. It includes the temporal, infratemporal and submasseteric spaces, and communicates with the submandibular and parapharyngeal spaces.

Temporal space

Location

  • Between fascia and muscle, anterior to temporalis
  • Superiorly: the temporal line
  • Inferiorly: the zygomatic arch and infratemporal crest

Contents & communications

  • Fat
  • Infratemporal space, submasseteric space

Infratemporal space

In the infratemporal fossa, adjacent to the lateral pterygoid plate and maxillary tuberosity.

DirectionBoundary
LaterallyMedial surface of the mandible and temporalis
RoofInfratemporal surface of the greater wing of the sphenoid
MediallyAnteriorly the lateral pterygoid plate; posteriorly the pharynx, with tensor and levator veli palatini and the superior constrictor
PosteriorlyCarotid sheath
AnteriorlyPosterior border of the maxillary sinus

Contents

  • Maxillary artery and branches
  • Mandibular nerve and branches
  • Pterygoid plexus of veins

Communicates with

  • Temporal, submasseteric, submandibular and parapharyngeal spaces

Pterygomandibular space

Part of the infratemporal space, between the medial pterygoid muscle and the mandibular ramus.

Boundaries

  • Laterally: medial surface of the mandibular ramus
  • Medially: medial pterygoid
  • Superiorly: lateral pterygoid
  • Anteriorly: pterygomandibular raphe
  • Posteriorly: parotid gland

Contents

  • Inferior alveolar nerve, artery and vein
  • Lingual nerve
  • Sphenomandibular ligament
  • Mylohyoid nerve, artery and vein

Communicates with the submandibular and parapharyngeal spaces.

This is the space you inject into. An inferior alveolar nerve block deposits solution in the pterygomandibular space, which is why its contents read like the list of structures an IANB anaesthetises. It also explains two complications: injecting too deeply or posteriorly reaches the parotid gland and anaesthetises the facial nerve, giving a temporary facial palsy; and puncturing the pterygoid venous plexus causes a haematoma.

Submasseteric space

  • Between the masseter muscle and the lateral surface of the mandibular ramus
  • Communicates with the temporal, infratemporal and pterygomandibular spaces
Why submasseteric infection causes trismus: pus between masseter and the ramus makes the muscle splint. Marked trismus after a lower third molar infection is a warning sign, not just discomfort.

Lecture 13 · Part 5Spaces Around the Floor of the Mouth

Submental space

Midline, between the mandibular symphysis and the hyoid bone.

Boundaries

  • Superior: mylohyoid
  • Inferior: hyoid musculature
  • Lateral: anterior belly of digastric

Contents & communications

  • Anterior jugular veins, submental lymph nodes
  • Communicates with the submandibular and sublingual spaces, and the thoracic inlet

Submandibular space

Lateral and posterior to the submental space, bilaterally.

Boundaries

  • Superior: mylohyoid
  • Lateral: mandible, platysma
  • Medial: hyoglossus
  • Inferior: digastric

Contents & communications

  • Submandibular salivary gland and lymph nodes
  • Part of the facial artery
  • Communicates with the submental, sublingual, infratemporal and parapharyngeal spaces

Sublingual space

Deep in the oral cavity, with mylohyoid forming its floor.

Boundaries

  • Superior: mucosa
  • Anterolateral: mandible
  • Medial: genioglossus
  • Posterior: hyoid bone

Contents

  • Part of the submandibular gland; the sublingual gland
  • Wharton's duct
  • Lingual nerve and vessels
  • Hypoglossal nerve
Mylohyoid decides everything here. Whether a lower tooth's infection goes into the sublingual space (above mylohyoid) or the submandibular space (below it) depends on whether the root apex lies above or below the mylohyoid line. Molars sit below, so they drain submandibularly; premolars and anteriors sit above.
Ludwig's angina is bilateral infection of the submandibular, sublingual and submental spaces at once. The floor of the mouth is pushed up and back, the tongue is elevated, and the airway is threatened. It is the reason this lecture exists — and it usually starts with a lower molar.
